authors.biography:
Alexei Drummond is Professor of Computational Biology at the University of Auckland, in the Schools of Biological Sciences and Computer Science. For more than two decades his group has developed Bayesian statistical methods for phylogenetics, phylodynamics and population genetics, and implemented them in the BEAST software platform (https://beast2.org). He was the founding Director of the Centre for Computational Evolution (2016-2022).

BEAST is widely used to analyse genetic and evolutionary data in fields from epidemiology to palaeontology and linguistics, and the main BEAST software papers have been cited more than 44,000 times. His current work is on the next generation of this infrastructure: BEAST 3, a modernised BEAST platform, and PhyloSpec, a model specification language that lets researchers, and AI agents, describe a phylogenetic model once and run inference across multiple engines.

He is a Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand.

Short Bio

I am a molecular biologist by training (Toulouse, FR). I did my Ph.D. at EMBL (Heidelberg, GE) and EMBL-EBI (Cambridge, UK) under the supervision of Des Higgins. In 2001, I became a CNRS fellow and since 2007 I have been a senior PI at the CRG (Barcelona, ES) where I manage a team of about 10 researchers. My most notable scientific achievements include:

Nextflow, a pipeline language that makes it possible to run complex analyses in a portable and reproducible way (www.nextflow.io, Nature Biotech 2017). In 2021, Nextflow was awarded the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics innovation award. While in my lab, four of my students incorporated two highly successful companies around this new technology: Lifebits (Chatzou, Prieto) and Seqera Labs (Floden, DiTomasso). Altogether these two companies had already raised over 100 million dollars in 2022. 

T-Coffee, a multiple sequence alignment algorithm (www.tcoffee.org, JMB 2000, Nature Biotech 2019) that has received over 8.000 citations and whose consistency-based algorithm now forms the basis of most multiple sequence aligners. 

NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics, a sister title of Nucleic Acids Research that I launched in 2019, with the support of NAR and Oxford University Press. I act as a chief editor in this journal that specializes in publishing methods with a strong focus on reproducibility. 

"Bioinformatics for Dummies", a title of the dummies series that I co-authored with Jean-Michel Claverie  (2002, 2009). The book has been one of the best-selling titles of bioinformatics with over 40.0000 copies sold worldwide.

My scientific interests are very wide and include any domain where sequence comparison methods can contribute: sequence analysis algorithm, phylogeny reconstruction methods, rational use of structural information for sequence and evolutionary analysis, genomics and transcriptomics analysis, RNA analysis algorithms, methodological development for longitudinal data analysis and high-throughput computation. 

I am a huge fan of informal inter-disciplinary adventures and even though I am growing wiser by the years, I still find it hard to resist crazy collaboration invitations by fellow scientists. In this domain, my most adventurous expedition has probably been the adaptation of bioinformatics methods for the analysis of social longitudinal data, in collaboration with Lausanne University Social Science department. I am not ruling out even wilder endeavors in the future - on the contrary...

Jonathan is a postdoctoral researcher in the discipline of Mathematics within the School of Natural Sciences at the University of Tasmania and the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Plant Success in Nature and Agriculture.

Jonathan’s training is in mathematical and statistical phylogenetics. He is developing mathematical models of convergent evolution in plant species of interest to the Centre of Excellence, including Sorghum and Senecio. Key problems of interest include determining which genes or sections of genomes have evolved in similar ways due to similar selective pressures and how these genetic similarities are associated with plant function.

Jonathan completed his undergraduate and PhD degrees at the University of Tasmania. He was then a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Alaska Fairbanks in Fairbanks, USA and Institut Pasteur in Paris, before returning to the University of Tasmania for his current postdoctoral research position.

With his University of Alaska Fairbanks colleagues, Jonathan is developing new statistical tests and model selection procedures for the multispecies coalescent model of incomplete lineage sorting and implementing them in the R package MSCquartets.

authors.biography:
Constantinos (aka "Costis" with an accent on 'i') Daskalakis is a Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT. He holds a Diploma in Electrical and Computer Engineering from the National Technical University of Athens, and a PhD in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from UC Berkeley. He works on Computation Theory and its interface with Machine Learning, Game Theory, Economics, Probability Theory and Statistics. He has resolved long-standing open problems about the computational complexity of Nash equilibrium, and the mathematical structure and computational complexity of multi-item auctions. His current work focuses on high-dimensional statistics, multi-agent learning, learning from biased and dependent data, causal inference, econometrics, and Generative AI, particularly Diffusion Models. 

He has been honored with the ACM Doctoral Dissertation Award, the Kalai Prize from the Game Theory Society, the Sloan Fellowship in Computer Science, the SIAM Outstanding Paper Prize, the Microsoft Research Faculty Fellowship, the Simons Investigator Award, the Rolf Nevanlinna Prize from the International Mathematical Union, the ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award, the Bodossaki Foundation Distinguished Young Scientists Award, the ACM SIGECOM Test of Time Award, the 2022 Test of Time Award from Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, and the 2026 Test of Time Award from the Symposium on the Theory of Computing (STOC) conference. He is an ACM fellow, holds an honorary doctorate from the University of Patras and an honorary professorship at the University of Piraeus, and was awarded the Golden Cross of the Order of the Redeemer by the Greek Presidency. He has served in the scientific and advisory board of the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing (2018-2020), and as the head of the theory of computation group at MIT (2018-2022). He is a co-founder of Archimedes AI research center where he maintains the role of chief scientist. He chaired the AI strategy committee for the Greek Prime Minister. He is a cofounder and chief scientist at Percepta AI.

I am a Professor at the Departments of Biological Sciences and of Biomedical Informatics at Vanderbilt University and holder of the Cornelius Vanderbilt Chair in Biological Sciences. I also serve as the Founding Director of the Vanderbilt Evolutionary Studies Initiative (http://www.vanderbilt.edu/evolution), an interdisciplinary center that unites scholars from diverse disciplines with broad interests and expertise in evolution-related fields. I received my undergraduate degree in Biology from the University of Crete, Greece (1998) and my PhD from Edinburgh University, Scotland (2001). Prior to joining Vanderbilt in the summer of 2007, I was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (2002–2005) and a research scientist at the Broad Institute (2005–2007). I have written about my personal path in science in a Q & A article in Current Biology (vol. 35: R939 - R942).

Research in my laboratory focuses on the study of the DNA record to gain insight into the patterns and processes of evolution. Through a combination of computational and experimental approaches, my laboratory’s current research aims to understand the molecular foundations of the fungal lifestyle, the reconstruction of the tree of life, and the evolution of human pregnancy. 

My team’s research has been recognized by many awards, including a Searle Scholarship (2008), an NSF CAREER award (2009), an endowed chair (2013), and fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation (2018), the American Academy of Microbiology (2019), and the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) (2020). Finally, the Vanderbilt Evolutionary Studies Initiative has been recognized by the “Friend of Darwin” award (2025), presented by the National Center for Science Education to individuals or organizations that have substantially contributed to evolution education.

authors.biography:
Nadia Tahiri is particularly interested in establishing the mathematical and statistical foundations for solving the difficult problem of phylogenetic tree classification and creating a new open-source platform for biologists to use our new methods. She will define new optimization criteria for the construction of multiple alternative consensus trees and supertrees using clustering algorithms and several important phylogenetic tree metrics. The team proposes the following three main thrusts to create a computational framework to study gene evolutionary history: (1) the development of new efficient algorithms to classify and construct a plausible set of several alternative consensus trees and supertrees characterizing the available data, (2) the exploration of evolutionary patterns of Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and (3) the design and implementation of a new opensource software platform containing all the algorithms developed in our research lab as well as real and simulated data.

The long-term goal of our research lab is to develop an innovative systematic and automated approach to reconstruct different scenarios of the genetic evolution of other species groups affected by reticulate evolutionary events. For example, our research will contribute to the inference of multiple alternative subtrees of the tree of life that gathers crucial information about the biodiversity and evolutionary relationships of all living organisms.

authors.biography:
My research group has two main areas of expertise: RNA bioinformatics and the development of computational methods and reproducible analysis pipelines for high-throughput sequencing (HTS) data. My chair is internationally recognized as one of the leading groups in RNA bioinformatics, both for developing algorithms to solve complex optimization problems in RNA structure analysis and design and for developing dedicated computational methods to identify and predict RNA–protein and RNA–RNA interactions from sequencing data. In recent years, we have increasingly combined classical algorithmic approaches with advanced artificial intelligence and machine-learning methods, including deep learning, transformers and biological foundation models. These methods are applied to problems ranging from RNA structure prediction and RNA design to the prediction of molecular interactions and the analysis of large-scale sequencing data.

CRISPR bioinformatics has developed into a second major methodological focus of my group. Our work covers the identification, annotation, classification and evolutionary analysis of CRISPR-Cas systems, including CRISPR arrays, Cas proteins, tracrRNAs and anti-CRISPR proteins. More recently, we have expanded this research towards AI-based approaches for CRISPR/Cas off-target prediction and their systematic benchmarking for genome-editing safety. Our group is internationally well established in CRISPR bioinformatics through its contributions to the classification and evolutionary understanding of CRISPR-Cas systems as well as through the development of computational tools for their systematic analysis.

A further major focus is the development of robust, scalable and reproducible pipelines for sequencing-based research. This includes workflows for bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, genomics, epigenomics, metagenomics and microbial sequence analysis. Here, as well as in the topics mentioned above, it is always important for me not just to develop tools, but to cooperate with experimental groups. For that reason, most of my publications are the result of these collaborations.

My main areas come together in the RNA Bioinformatics Center of the German Network for Bioinformatics Infrastructure (de.NBI), which I coordinate. Within this infrastructure, we develop, maintain and provide reproducible analysis workflows for RNA-based data and a broad range of other high-throughput sequencing technologies including single-cell sequencing and metagenomics. The chair is also responsible for the European Galaxy server, useGalaxy.eu, which has developed into the largest Galaxy instance in Europe and one of the largest worldwide. It has more than 150.000 users and provides, for free, access to more than 4000 installed tools and major public databases, as well as associated training courses. This server got recently permanent support from the Ministry of Science, Research and the Arts (MWK) and the University of Freiburg.

The development of de novo methodology to study breast cancer [2024 citations; 54 publications]. My lab has a long-standing interest in the development of gene signatures in breast cancer. Gene signatures use, for example, mRNA levels for a (small) set of genes in a multivariate fashion to classify or stratify patients relative to a clinical endpoint eg prognosis or benefit from a therapy. We have also developed de novo frameworks such as BreSAT (Breast Signatures Analysis Tool), AIMS (Absolute Inference of Molecular Subtype, and AIPS (Absolute Inference of Patient Signatures). This work has been supported by funding from Genome Quebec/Canada, the NIH, and the CIHR. The methodology development here will be supported by machines from this CFI.

The development of bioinformatics and genomic technologies for chemical genomic profiling and phenotypic heterogeneity in fungal model organisms [943 citations]. We generated ~10 manuscripts describing novel bioinformatics and experimental methodology in the context of high-throughput genomic screens and microscopy with model organisms including Yeast and Candida. This included an effort to predict chemical synergy in fungi. Recently, our group was the first to successfully profile the opportunistic human pathogen Candida albicans at the transcriptional level, and we recently developed a deep learning based approach to dissect morphology of the human pathogen C. albicans from microscopy images.

Modifications of these approaches are directly applicable here in this project that will build upon multiple animal models for infectious disease and cognitive disabilities. authors.biography: I am a bioinformatician by training with a strong interest in the evolutionary processes that shape microbial and viral genomes. Viruses are central players in microbial communities and viruses also have a major effect on communities of eukaryotic organisms. This interaction has important consequences for the evolution of cellular organisms. We now have the technology to measure the genetic content of communities at high resolution and we can infer which organisms with which detailed genome organization they contain, including all community members - eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses. In my research group, we develop methods for the reconstruction of genomes and their evolutionary histories and gain biological insights by analyzing data with these methods. Specifically, we develop and apply approaches (i) to reconstruct viruses from metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data and (ii) to infer microbial population genetic processes from genomic and metagenomic data.

Tiziano Leidi is a professor and director at the Institute of Information Systems and Networking (ISIN) at the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI). After obtaining his diploma in Computer Science from ETH Zurich in 1999, Professor Leidi has developed a career that bridges academic teaching and research in the fields of computer science and engineering. His professional focus includes advanced programming techniques, software architectures, and digital signal processing, with a particular interest in parallel computing, audio-visual computing, domain-specific languages, real-time stream processing, and GPU programming.
Leidi's approach to applied research is characterized by pragmatic engagement with technology's potential to address real-world problems. His pursuit of a PhD as a part-time study, completed in 2012, reflects a deep commitment to bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and its practical applications. Through his doctoral studies, Leidi sought to explore the practical implications of advanced software-design and programming techniques in solving specific, applied issues, demonstrating his dedication to impactful research.
His recent research activities aim to advance understanding and innovation within his fields of interest. A noteworthy achievement in Leidi's recent career is his contribution to the development of 3D audio technologies, particularly in the area of cross-talk cancellation. This work has culminated in scientific publications and an international patent, marking a milestone in audio technology. The published methodology improves the spatial audio experience, showcasing Leidi's commitment to advancing technological frontiers with applied research.
At SUPSI, Professor Leidi contributes to the development of curricula that prepare students for future professional challenges. As director of the Institute for Information Systems and Networking, he oversees projects and initiatives aimed at enhancing the institute's research output and educational offerings. Professor Leidi's work demonstrates a commitment to fostering an environment where students and researchers can thrive, innovate, and contribute to advancements in technology and computer science. In his career, Professor Leidi has maintained a balance between academic rigor, research innovation, and the practical application of computing technologies. He has authored and co-authored several publications that explore various aspects of multimedia processing, computer simulation, and performance optimization, contributing to the academic community's body of knowledge. His contributions to SUPSI and the broader academic community highlight the importance of interdisciplinary approaches to solving complex problems in the ICT sector.

authors.biography: Guillermo López Taboada (Lalín, Spain, 1979) received his B.S.-M.S. (2002) and PhD (2009) in Informatics, both at the University of A Coruña (UDC), Spain.  He completed his education through research visits to the University of Portsmouth (UK), Manchester Metropolitan University (UK) and Accenture Fintech Lab (UK). He has been teaching at the Faculty of Computer Science of UDC since 2004 and was promoted to the position of Full Professor (since 2022).  His main research interests are in the convergence of Cloud computing and Big Data processing, covering in nearly 20 years of experience: software tools for Big Data and Cloud Computing, HPC/Cloud/Big Data infrastructures, and cloud applications (currently focusing on data science applications on Data Lakes). He has published 29 JCR journal papers in the last 10 years. He has also supervised 5 PhD Theses (all with the International Mention and 3 awarded as Best PhD Thesis). Moreover, he is PI of contracts with companies on cloud computing and Big Data, most on them using Data Lakes, as enablers of the digital transformation of industry, particularly in smart cities/mobility, e-learning, energy management systems, and sustainability. Overall, he has participated in 43 national and international R&D and technology transfer projects, contracts, and networks, funded by competitive public calls or by private agreements. He has been PI or co-PI in 17 of them. Since 2013, Dr. Taboada acts as CEO of Torus, the UDC spin-off company primarily focused on the design and deployment of cloud-based automation and Data Lakes.  Torus has received 18 entrepreneurship awards, including the "Ramón LLull" Spanish National Computer Science Award in 2020. He is coauthor of one US patent and has registered 4 software products in the IP Registry.  Finally, he has contributed as invited keynote or roundtable speaker in 9 national and international events since 2017, mainly on the topics of cloud computing and Big Data as enablers of the digital transformation of industry.
